list.listitem: Eventual spontaneous resolution is normal for immunocompetent patients, so expectant management is a reasonable option. B
Treatment with topical salicylic acid and/or cryotherapy produces cure rates between 50% and 60% within weeks to months, compared to placebo which yields a cure rate of about 23%. B

While topical salicylic acid (SA) only has modest efficacy, studies supporting its effectiveness are more consistent than those for cryotherapy. Additinoally, SA probably causes less adverse events than cryotherapy. A

Cryotherapy, based on meta-analysis, does not appear better than placebo but has similar efficacy to SA. Aggressive cryotherapy (ie, duration >10-15 seconds or performed at least twice) appears more effective than gentle cryotherapy but leads to more adverse events. Monthly cryotherapy produces comparable results to shorter treatment intervals. For hand warts, cryotherapy may be more effective than SA. Furthermore, combined cryotherapy and SA may produce better outcomes than either treatment alone. B

background.definition: Warts are the cutaneous response to an infection with the human papilloma virus. Plantar warts describe warts that occur on the soles of the feet. Flat warts most commonly occur on the face, hands, and the lower legs of women who shave.

list.listitem: Twenty-two percent (222/1000) of 2491 school-aged Australian children were found to have warts.
Other studies show a range of prevalence from 0.84% to 24% (8.4-240 per 1000 persons).
Plantar warts—mainly human papillomavirus type 1, although 2, 3, 4, 27, 29, 57, 60, 63, 65, 66 and 69 have been found.
Flat warts—human papillomavirus types 3, 10, 28, and 49.
Warts are a viral infection.
Warts usually regress spontaneously in immunocompetent patients.
The diagnosis of warts is based on clinical appearance, ranging from flat, to filiform, dome shaped, or growing down into the plantar or palmar surfaces. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Do not have black dots on paring. Skin lines run through them; skin lines run around plantar warts.
Can appear similar to flat warts. The distribution is different from that of flat warts; the most common sites are the ankles, wrists, and back.
Flat seborrheic keratoses can look like large flat warts. Their larger size and smaller numbers help to distinguish these from the flat warts.

list.listitem: Flat or plantar warts typically present as nonpigmented cutaneous lesions that persist for months or years.

Plantar warts, found on the soles of the feet, are firm, raised lesions that are tender to direct pressure. Paring them with a scalpel reveals telltale punctate dots which are thrombosed blood vessels in cross section.

Flat warts are flesh colored and usually occur in clusters on the face, hands, or legs in those who shave their legs. They can be seen in a linear pattern due to the microtrauma of shaving or they can be spread by scratching.
Shave biopsy is recommended if the lesion is suspicious for malignancy or if the diagnosis is in question.
The diagnosis of warts is almost always clinical. See the section History and Physical for more detail.
Biopsy is only necessary when the diagnosis is uncertain or skin malignancy is suspected because of location or appearance.

Many warts will spontaneously resolve, so treatment is not mandatory. If the patient requests treatment, try topical salicylic acid first as it is more cost effective and can be used at home. Cryotherapy is a good second-line therapy, and may be preferable if patients prefer more immediate results.
If a patient desires treatment for warts instead of waiting for spontaneous resolution, suggest daily application of topical salicylic acid. A

Cryotherapy, based on meta-analysis, does not appear better than placebo but has similar efficacy to SA. Aggressive cryotherapy (ie, duration >10-15 seconds or performed at least twice) appears more effective than gentle cryotherapy but leads to more adverse events. Monthly cryotherapy produces comparable results to shorter treatment intervals. For hand warts, cryotherapy may be more effective than SA. Furthermore, combined cryotherapy and SA may produce better outcomes than either treatment alone. B
Dinitrochlorobenzene (DNCB) may be more effective than placebo, but is not widely available. B
Clear duct tape is no better than placebo. B

There is insufficient evidence to support the use of topical zinc, silver nitrate, 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), phenol, or imiquimod; intralesional 5-FU, bleomycin, or antigen; and pulsed dye laser or photodynamic therapy. B
No RCTs have evaluated the efficacy of formaldehyde, podophyllotoxin, cantharidin, excision, or curettage. B

The British Association of Dermatologists guidelines recommend salicylic acid and/or cryotherapy as having the highest strength of evidence to support them. Other treatments with much lower levels of evidence include dithranol, 5-FU, formaldehyde, hyperthermia, laser, and podophyllotoxin. For hand warts, salicylic acid is most strongly recommended, followed by cryotherapy, and then either bleomycin, contact immunotherapy, 5-FU or laser. They specifically recommend against using painful treatments if possible, as most warts will clear spontaneously within 1 to 2 years.

For plantar warts, topical salicylic acid treatments by topical liquid, patch, or applicator stick appear effective, with a risk ratio for clearance of warts at all sites of 1.6 (95% CI 1.2-2.0). It may be more effective for hands (RR 2.7) than feet (RR 1.3). Apply daily topical 17% salicylic acid liquid or rub on with applicator "Wart Stick" under occlusion to the wart(s), or apply salicylic-impregnated patch every 2 days to 3 days until the wart(s) resolve. Resolution may take weeks to months. Soaking the area and debulking the wart with a pumice stone or file may facilitate removal of overlying skin and increase the effect of the acid on the wart.

A Dutch RCT studied 13 week treatment protocols in adults and children with common (n = 188) or plantar (n = 227) warts. They compared cryotherapy with monochloroacetic acid (MCA) applied in the office every 2 weeks for common warts, and MCA with cryotherapy plus daily salicylic acid (SA) application for plantar warts. After 13 weeks, cure rates were similar between groups for common warts (43% for MCA vs 54% for cryotherapy) and for plantar warts (46% for MCA vs 39% for cryo + SA). They conclude that office applied MCA every 2 weeks is a reasonable alternative to more traditional treatment approaches.
A British RCT compared cryotherapy with daily application of salicylic acid for plantar warts (n = 240) and found no difference in clearance rates, number of warts, or time to clearance.

A systematic review of 12 studies on warts showed significant clearance of warts with topical cantharidin only. In combination with podophyllotoxin and salicyclic acid, cantharidin demonstrated efficacy for plantar warts (pediatric and adult; clearance rate range 81-100%; 4 studies had 100% clearance) with majority clearing after single treatment. Pain, blistering and hyper/hypopigmentation were most common adverse effects.

Dinitrochlorobenzene (DNCB) as a contact sensitizer, 5-fluorouracil, intralesional interferon, and photodynamic therapy show evidence for limited efficacy, but are potentially hazardous or toxic. Bleomycin was not found to be consistently effective.

Small studies have reported success with injecting either mumps antigen or Candida antigen, theoretically to induce an immune response. One regimen used candida antigen 1:1 mixture with 1% lidocaine 0.1 mL per wart, up to 1 mL every 4 weeks until the wart resolved or a maximum of 3 injections, with a 72% resolution rate.

For flat warts, treat as above with topical salicylates. Be cautious to avoid the eyes. Topical imiquimod has some effect according to small trials and case reports. Topical tretinoin has been recommended for flat warts but no clinical trials were identified.
There is no evidence to support the use of systematic therapies such as cimetidine, levamisole, homeopathy, or zinc.

A network meta-analysis of 17 RCTs compared intralesional immunotherapy modalities to cryotherapy, imiquimod, or placebo for treatment of warts. They conclude purified protein derivative vaccine (PPD) and measles, mumps, rubella vaccine (MMR) were the most efective in achieving complete primary and distant recovery and reducing the recurrence rate at the same site compared with other immunotherapuetic modalities and cryotherapy.

Cryotherapy is frequently used in the treatment of warts on the basis of clinical experience and trials that compared different methods instead of against placebo. Cryotherapy was comparable in efficacy to salicylic acid in a Cochrane review and in a recent study of 240 patients. More aggressive cryotherapy is more effective, but also causes more adverse effects.

In a small trial, oral zinc therapy at 10 mg/kg per day to a maximum of 600 mg per day resulted in 86.9% clearance rate in the 40 treated patients compared with 13.3% in the 40 placebo-control patients.

Duct tape therapy has been tried, but is not significantly more effective than nontreatment. A Cochrane review found two studies of duct tape with 193 participants, but no overall benefit compared with placebo (RR 1.4, 95% CI 0.5-4.0).
A small study found that hypnotherapy was more effective than salicylates or no treatment.
A single small trial found that acupuncture was more effective than tretinoin ointment (53% clearing vs 3%).
A case series of 30 patients found a 63% response rate using palm leaf based ointment. Randomized trial evidence is lacking.
Consider referring to dermatology any immunocompromised patient with extensive warts who does not respond to initial treatments.
Cryotherapy can cause erythema, pain, and blistering. The wart may not resolve or may require repeat treatments. Uncommonly, deep structures, including nerves, may be damaged by the cryotherapy.
Treatment with Candida antigen can cause systemic symptoms similar to a viral syndrome due to stimulating an immune response.
Sensitization treatment with DNCB can cause significant inflammation.
Treatment with curettage, laser, or electrosurgery can cause large defects in the skin and subsequent scarring.
Occlusive treatments, including duct tape and topical acids, can cause irritation of the surrounding skin.
Eventual spontaneous resolution is normal for immunocompetent patients. B
Approximately half of children with warts will be free of warts 1 year later, even without treatment. B
Treatment with topical salicylic acid and/or cryotherapy produces cure rates between 50% and 60% within weeks to months, compared to placebo which yields a cure rate of about 23%. B

The HPV type appears to influence prognosis. In a Dutch study, 58% of HPV-1 associated warts spontaneously resolved, compared with 3% to 7% for other types. Response to cryotherapy or salicylic acid also varied by type. B
Patients with immune deficiencies due to systemic illness or therapy will often have larger numbers of warts that are more recalcitrant to therapy.
